claims.text: RHEAs with unprotected surfaces are susceptible to degradation in high-temperature oxidative environments.
A reactive force field can be specifically calibrated to capture oxide-scale formation kinetics on an alloy surface.
Quantum-mechanical and atomistic simulation techniques can be used to develop the proposed reactive force field.
Applicable force fields for computational investigation of HEAs have been limited.
Classical force-field simulations of an Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni HEA can reproduce selected structural properties obtained from first-principles calculations and experiments.
Force fields not optimized for oxide-scale kinetics provide less accurate oxidation predictions.
Standard non-reactive force fields do not reliably guide the design of protective RHEAs.
Oxide-scale formation strongly influences RHEA oxidation behavior at 1000–1100 °C.
Failure to form a dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer at 1000 °C can produce exponentially increasing weight gain.
Formation of a protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer at 1100 °C is associated with parabolic oxidation behavior and comparatively high oxidation resistance.
A dense, continuous oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
The proposed reactive force field will capture oxide nucleation, growth, and stabilization atomistically.
Simulating oxide nucleation, growth, and stabilization will enable assessment of whether the oxide microstructure is an effective oxidation barrier.
The proposed reactive force field will accurately predict formation of a dense, protective oxide layer on RHEAs.
Reactive-force-field simulations will predict protective oxide-scale kinetics more accurately than standard non-reactive force-field models.
Accurate prediction of protective oxide formation can guide alloy design toward improved high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Oxide thickness, growth rate, composition, and weight gain over time can be compared between simulation and oxidation experiments to validate the force field.
A deviation greater than 20% in growth kinetics or a mismatch in protective oxide phases would falsify the proposed model-adequacy hypothesis.
